meta.subject: STATISTICS
meta.author: bank-team-statistics
meta.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.learningObjective: Identify the median of a small data set
questions.stem: An amateur astronomer logs nightly star counts of 3, 7, 9, 12, 40 over five nights; which value is the median?

options.text: The middle value after sorting the five counts is 9
The mean of all five nightly counts is about 14.2
The smallest nightly count 3 is the median
options.misconception: picks the minimum instead of middle

options.text: The largest nightly count 40 is the median
options.misconception: picks the maximum instead of middle

questions.explanation: Sorting gives 3, 7, 9, 12, 40, so the middle value is 9. The mean differs because of the outlier 40, and min or max are not middle values.
questions.hint: Sort the data first, then take the middle.

questions.learningObjective: Compute the range of a data set
questions.stem: An amateur astronomer records meteor counts 5, 11, 14, 20, 23 over five nights; what is the range?
questions.explanation: Range equals maximum minus minimum, so 23 minus 5 equals 18. It measures total spread from smallest to largest observation.
questions.hint: Subtract the smallest from the largest.

questions.stem: An amateur astronomer plots a histogram of star magnitudes that tails off toward the bright end; describe the skewness.

answer.exemplar: The distribution is skewed left because the tail extends toward lower magnitudes, pulling the mean below the median.

questions.explanation: A tail toward lower values indicates left skew, where the mean is pulled below the median. The bulk of data concentrates on the right side.
questions.hint: The tail direction names the skew.

questions.learningObjective: Classify a variable as categorical or quantitative
questions.stem: An amateur astronomer records the constellation name seen each night; what type of variable is this?

options.text: It is a quantitative variable measured in counts
It is a categorical variable with no natural order
It is a quantitative variable with units of stars
It is a binary variable with two outcomes

questions.explanation: Constellation names are labels without numeric value, so the variable is categorical. Counting stars would be quantitative, but names are not counts.
questions.hint: Ask whether arithmetic on values makes sense.

questions.learningObjective: Choose an appropriate display for categorical data
questions.stem: An amateur astronomer wants to show counts of meteors by color category; which display fits best?

options.text: A scatterplot of color against time
A histogram with equal-width numeric bins
A bar chart with one bar per color category
A boxplot of the color labels

questions.explanation: Bar charts display counts for distinct categories clearly. Histograms and boxplots require numeric data, so they are inappropriate for color labels.
questions.hint: Match the display to the variable type.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why the median resists outliers
questions.stem: An amateur astronomer includes one night with 200 meteors; why does the median stay more stable than the mean?

answer.exemplar: The median depends only on the middle position, so one extreme value changes it little, while the mean uses every value and shifts toward the outlier.

questions.explanation: The median uses only middle positions, so extremes barely move it. The mean averages all values, so a large outlier pulls it strongly toward itself.
questions.hint: Count how many values each measure uses.

questions.stem: An amateur astronomer compares two nights: Night A counts 8,9,10,11,12 and Night B counts 2,4,10,16,18; which night has the larger center?

options.text: Night A has the larger center at about 10
Spread determines which center is larger
Both nights share the same center 10
Night B has the larger center at about 11

questions.explanation: Night A mean is 10 and Night B mean is 11, so Night B has the larger center. Spread differs but does not change which mean is larger.

questions.stem: An amateur astronomer's histogram shows 12 stars in the 0-5 magnitude bin and 8 stars in the 5-10 bin; how many stars total in those two bins?
questions.explanation: Adding the two bin counts gives 12 plus 8 equals 20 stars. Histogram bins partition observations without overlap.

questions.stem: An amateur astronomer's boxplot reports min 4, Q1 7, median 10, Q3 14, max 19; which value is Q3?

options.text: Q3 is the third quartile value 14

questions.explanation: The five-number summary lists min, Q1, median, Q3, max in order, so Q3 is 14. Maximum and median are separate entries.

questions.learningObjective: Combine center and spread in a description
questions.stem: An amateur astronomer describes a cluster of galaxy distances; what two features must the description include?

answer.exemplar: A good description states a measure of center such as the mean or median and a measure of spread such as the standard deviation or IQR.

questions.explanation: Describing a distribution requires both center and spread. Center alone hides variability, and spread alone hides location.

questions.learningObjective: Compute the mean of a data set
questions.stem: An amateur astronomer logs star counts 6, 8, 10, 12, 14 over five nights; what is the mean?
questions.explanation: Sum is 50 and there are five values, so the mean is 10. The symmetric data make the mean equal to the median.
questions.hint: Divide the sum by the count.

questions.stem: An amateur astronomer's data have Q1 12 and Q3 28; what is the interquartile range?
questions.explanation: IQR equals Q3 minus Q1, so 28 minus 12 equals 16. It captures the middle half of the data.

questions.learningObjective: Match skew direction to mean and median
questions.stem: An amateur astronomer finds a right-skewed distribution of meteor counts; which relation holds?

options.text: Median exceeds mean in right skew
Mean is less than median in right skew
Mean equals median in right skew
Mean is greater than median in right skew

questions.explanation: Right skew has a tail toward high values, pulling the mean above the median. Left skew pulls the mean below the median.

questions.stem: An amateur astronomer measures the exact temperature of a telescope mirror; what type is this variable?

options.misconception: treats any count-like measure as discrete

questions.explanation: Temperature can take any value in a range, so it is continuous. Discrete variables take countable values like whole stars.
questions.hint: Can it take any value in an interval?

questions.stem: An amateur astronomer's stem-and-leaf shows stem 3 with leaves 2,5,7; what are the three data values?
questions.explanation: In a stem-and-leaf plot the stem is the tens digit and each leaf is a ones digit, giving 32, 35, 37. Reversing or splitting digits misreads the plot.
questions.hint: Stem is tens, leaf is ones.

questions.learningObjective: Compute the mean with an outlier
questions.stem: An amateur astronomer logs four nights 10, 10, 10, 10 plus one night 60; what is the mean?
questions.explanation: Sum is 100 across five nights, so the mean is 20. The single outlier 60 raises the mean far above the typical 10.
questions.hint: Sum all five then divide by five.

questions.stem: An amateur astronomer compares two nights of counts; Night X 9,10,11 and Night Y 1,10,19; which is more variable?

options.text: Variability cannot be judged from three points
Night X is more variable with wider spread

options.misconception: assumes equal centers imply equal spread

options.text: Night Y is more variable with wider spread

questions.explanation: Night Y ranges from 1 to 19 while Night X ranges 9 to 11, so Night Y is more variable. Spread is visible in the range and clustering.
questions.hint: Look at how far values stray from center.

questions.stem: An amateur astronomer sees two peaks in a histogram of star brightness; what term applies?
questions.explanation: Two distinct peaks make a distribution bimodal. Unimodal has one peak and uniform has no peaks.

questions.learningObjective: Detect outliers using the 1.5 IQR rule
questions.stem: An amateur astronomer has Q1 10, Q3 20, and a value 45; is 45 an outlier by the 1.5 IQR rule?

options.text: No, 45 is below the upper fence
options.misconception: computes fence as Q3 plus IQR

questions.explanation: IQR is 10, so the upper fence is 20 plus 15 equals 35. Since 45 exceeds 35, it is an outlier.
questions.hint: Fence is Q3 plus 1.5 times IQR.

questions.stem: An amateur astronomer summarizes a data set; what three aspects should the summary mention?

answer.exemplar: The summary should mention shape, center, and spread, noting any outliers or gaps as deviations from the overall pattern.

questions.explanation: A full description covers shape, center, and spread, plus deviations like outliers. Omitting any aspect gives an incomplete picture.

questions.learningObjective: Choose mean or median for skewed data
questions.stem: An amateur astronomer has skewed meteor counts with one huge outlier night; which center measure is preferred?

options.text: The range is preferred for skewed data
The mean is preferred for skewed data
The mode is preferred for skewed data
The median is preferred for skewed data

questions.explanation: The median resists outliers and skew, making it preferred for skewed data. The mean is distorted by extremes.

questions.stem: An amateur astronomer records four star counts 2, 4, 6, 8; what is the sample standard deviation rounded to two decimals?
questions.explanation: Mean is 5; squared deviations sum to 20; divide by n minus 1 gives 6.666; square root is about 2.58. Sample SD uses n minus 1.
questions.hint: Use n minus 1 in the denominator.

questions.stem: An amateur astronomer's histogram of star counts is mirror-symmetric about its center; what shape is it?
questions.explanation: Mirror symmetry about the center defines a symmetric distribution. Skew requires an asymmetric tail.
questions.hint: Mirror image about center means symmetric.

questions.stem: An amateur astronomer rates seeing conditions as poor, fair, good, excellent; what variable type is this?
questions.explanation: Ratings have a natural order but unequal intervals, making them ordinal categorical. They are not numeric measurements.

questions.stem: An amateur astronomer wants to show the distribution of nightly star counts; which display is best?

options.text: A pie chart of the counts
A bar chart of each night
A histogram of the numeric counts

questions.explanation: A histogram displays the distribution of a quantitative variable. Pie and bar charts suit categorical data.

questions.learningObjective: Find median after removing an outlier
questions.stem: An amateur astronomer's five counts 3, 7, 9, 12, 40 have median 9; if 40 is removed, what is the new median of 3,7,9,12?
questions.explanation: With four values the median is the average of the two middle values, (7 plus 9) divided by 2 equals 8. Removing the outlier barely changes the median.

questions.stem: An amateur astronomer compares two months: Month P counts 5,6,7,8,9 and Month Q counts 1,2,9,16,17; which month has larger median?

options.text: Month Q has the larger median 3
Month P has the larger median 7
Month Q median exceeds Month P

questions.explanation: Month P median is 7 and Month Q median is 3, so Month P has the larger median. The means differ but medians are compared here.

questions.stem: An amateur astronomer's histogram bins show counts 5, 8, 7, 10 across four bins; what is the total number of observations?
questions.explanation: Summing all bin counts gives 5 plus 8 plus 7 plus 10 equals 30 observations. Each observation falls in exactly one bin.

questions.learningObjective: Read the median from a boxplot
questions.stem: An amateur astronomer's boxplot has median line at 15; what does this tell us?

options.text: The mean of all observations is 15

questions.explanation: The median splits the data in half, so about half the observations fall below 15. It need not equal the mean.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a gap in a distribution
questions.stem: An amateur astronomer notices an empty interval between two clusters of star counts; what is this called?

answer.exemplar: The empty interval is a gap, indicating a separation between two groups in the data that may reflect distinct populations.

questions.explanation: A gap is an interval with no observations, often signaling separate groups. It is a deviation worth noting in a description.
questions.hint: An empty interval between clusters is a gap.

questions.stem: An amateur astronomer weights three nights equally? Actually nights have 2, 4, 6 meteors with weights 1,2,3; what is the weighted mean?
questions.explanation: Weighted sum is 2*1 plus 4*2 plus 6*3 equals 28; total weight is 6; mean is 28/6 equals 4.6667. Weights change the contribution of each value.
questions.hint: Divide weighted sum by total weight.

questions.stem: An amateur astronomer's counts 4, 6, 8, 10 have mean 7; what is the mean absolute deviation?
questions.explanation: Absolute deviations from 7 are 3, 1, 1, 3 summing to 8; divided by 4 gives 2. MAD averages distance from the mean.

questions.stem: An amateur astronomer compares two symmetric distributions; larger IQR means what?

options.text: Greater spread in the middle half

questions.explanation: A larger IQR indicates greater spread among the middle 50 percent of data. It does not imply larger center or count.

questions.stem: An amateur astronomer counts the number of meteors per hour; what variable type is this?
questions.explanation: Meteor counts are whole numbers that can be counted, so the variable is discrete quantitative. It is not continuous or categorical.

questions.stem: An amateur astronomer's dotplot shows three dots above 8 and one dot above 12; how many observations are shown?
questions.explanation: Each dot represents one observation, so three plus one equals four. Values are positions, not counts.

questions.learningObjective: Explain effect of outlier on mean
questions.stem: An amateur astronomer adds one night with 500 meteors to data averaging 10; how does the mean change?

answer.exemplar: The mean increases substantially because the sum rises by 500 while the count rises by one, pulling the average upward toward the outlier.

questions.explanation: Adding a large value increases the sum much more than the count, so the mean rises toward the outlier. The median may barely move.

questions.stem: An amateur astronomer compares two histograms with same center but different spread; what differs?

options.misconception: assumes same center implies same shape

questions.explanation: Same center with different spread means one distribution is more variable. Center and sample size are unchanged by spread.

questions.stem: An amateur astronomer widens histogram bins; what happens to the number of bins?

options.text: The number of bins stays the same

questions.explanation: Wider bins cover more range per bin, so fewer bins are needed. The total observation count is unchanged.

questions.stem: An amateur astronomer sees a long box in a boxplot; what does that indicate?

options.text: The middle half is spread out

questions.explanation: Box length equals IQR, so a long box means the middle half of data is spread out. It does not indicate median size or count.

questions.learningObjective: Identify an outlier in a description
questions.stem: An amateur astronomer's star counts 5,6,7,8,50; which value is an outlier?

options.text: 5 is an outlier at the low end
8 is an outlier at the high end
50 is an outlier far from the cluster

questions.explanation: The value 50 lies far from the cluster 5-8, so it is an outlier. The minimum 5 is part of the cluster.
questions.hint: Look for values far from the cluster.

questions.learningObjective: Find mode of a data set
questions.stem: An amateur astronomer logs star counts 4, 4, 7, 9, 9, 9; what is the mode?
questions.explanation: The value 9 appears three times, more than any other, so the mode is 9. Mode is the most frequent value.

questions.stem: An amateur astronomer's counts range from 5 to 20; after adding a night with 25, what is the new range?
questions.explanation: New maximum is 25 and minimum stays 5, so range is 20. Wait 25-5=20. Yes. Adding the new max keeps range 20? Actually original 20-5=15; new 25-5=20. So 20. Good.
questions.hint: Subtract new min from new max.

questions.stem: An amateur astronomer's histogram has roughly equal bar heights; what shape is this?
questions.explanation: Roughly equal bar heights indicate an approximately uniform distribution. Skew requires a tail and bimodal requires two peaks.

questions.stem: An amateur astronomer measures exposure time in seconds; what variable type is this?
questions.explanation: Exposure time can take any value in an interval, so it is continuous quantitative. It is not a count or category.

questions.stem: An amateur astronomer's bar chart shows 15 meteors on Monday and 9 on Tuesday; how many more on Monday?
questions.explanation: Subtracting gives 15 minus 9 equals 6 more meteors on Monday. Adding would double count.

questions.stem: An amateur astronomer's four star counts are 4, 8, 12, 16; what is the median?
questions.explanation: With an even count the median is the average of the two middle values, (8 plus 12) divided by 2 equals 10.

questions.stem: An amateur astronomer compares two boxplots with same median but different IQR; what differs?

options.text: The spreads of the middle halves differ

questions.explanation: Equal medians mean equal centers, so the differing IQR means the middle-half spreads differ. Sample size is not shown by IQR.

questions.learningObjective: Locate the mode in a histogram
questions.stem: An amateur astronomer's histogram peaks at the 10-15 bin; what is the modal class?

options.text: The modal class is all bins
The modal class is the peak height 15

questions.explanation: The modal class is the bin with the highest frequency, here 10-15. Height alone is not a class.
questions.hint: Highest bar's bin is modal class.

questions.stem: An amateur astronomer has Q1 20 and Q3 32; what is the lower outlier fence?
questions.explanation: IQR is 12, so lower fence is 20 minus 1.5 times 12 equals 2. Values below 2 are outliers.
questions.hint: Lower fence is Q1 minus 1.5 IQR.

questions.stem: An amateur astronomer's data cluster tightly around 10 with one far value at 60; describe the pattern.

answer.exemplar: Most observations cluster tightly around 10, indicating a center near 10 with small spread, while the value 60 is a clear outlier.

questions.explanation: Tight clustering indicates small spread around center 10. The distant 60 deviates from this pattern and is an outlier.

questions.stem: An amateur astronomer sees values 5 (twice) and 10 (three times); what is the mean?
questions.explanation: Weighted sum is 5*2 plus 10*3 equals 40; total count is 5; mean is 8. Frequencies weight each value.

questions.stem: An amateur astronomer finds SD 2 for nightly counts; what does this indicate?

options.text: Counts typically vary about 2 from mean

questions.explanation: Standard deviation measures typical distance from the mean, so counts vary about 2 from the mean. It is not a max, mean, or count.
questions.hint: SD is typical distance from mean.

questions.stem: An amateur astronomer's data have a high outlier; what skew results?
questions.explanation: A high outlier creates a tail toward high values, producing right skew. Low outliers produce left skew.

questions.stem: An amateur astronomer measures distance to a star in light-years; what variable type is this?
questions.explanation: Distance has a true zero and meaningful ratios, so it is ratio quantitative. Temperature in Celsius would be interval.

questions.learningObjective: Choose display for two quantitative variables
questions.stem: An amateur astronomer wants to relate telescope aperture to star count; which display fits?

options.text: A pie chart of aperture values
A bar chart of counts only
A scatterplot of aperture versus count

questions.explanation: A scatterplot displays the relationship between two quantitative variables. Single-variable displays omit the relation.

questions.stem: An amateur astronomer's counts 2, 4, 6, 8, 100 have mean 24; excluding 100, what is the mean of the rest?
questions.explanation: Sum of 2,4,6,8 is 20 across four values, so the mean is 5. Removing the outlier restores the typical level.

questions.stem: An amateur astronomer compares two boxplots; Plot M median 12 and Plot N median 18; which has larger median?

options.text: Plot M has the larger median
Plot N has the larger median

questions.explanation: Plot N's median 18 exceeds Plot M's 12, so Plot N has the larger median. Boxplots display medians directly.

questions.stem: An amateur astronomer wants the median from a histogram; how can it be estimated?

answer.exemplar: Estimate the median as the value splitting the total area in half, using cumulative bin counts to find the middle observation.

questions.explanation: The median is the middle observation, found by accumulating bin counts until reaching half the total. Histogram bars give approximate counts.
questions.hint: Find the middle observation via cumulative counts.

questions.stem: An amateur astronomer sees a long upper whisker; what does it indicate?

options.text: High values spread far from Q3

options.misconception: assumes whisker length means no outliers

questions.explanation: Whiskers extend to non-outlier extremes, so a long upper whisker means high values spread far from Q3. It is not about median or box.

questions.stem: An amateur astronomer summarizes a distribution using SOCS; what does each letter stand for?

answer.exemplar: SOCS stands for Shape, Outliers, Center, and Spread, the four components of a complete distribution description.

questions.explanation: SOCS covers Shape, Outliers, Center, and Spread. Each component captures a different aspect of the distribution.
